leetcode.title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
leetcode.note: The **inverse** of Q11. LeetCode generates every letter string a number could spell; Q11 asks which *known words* it spells. Generating is exponential, looking up is O(1) - and noticing that the direction is reversed is the whole insight of Q11. Reader-reported independently.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Permutations
leetcode.note: Backtracking. No relation to any of the 17; a separately LinkedIn-tagged classic. Worth a rep because it is the template for "enumerate all arrangements".
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Permutations II
leetcode.note: Follow-up to 46: duplicates in the input. The de-duplication trick (sort, then skip a value equal to the previous one at the same depth) is the only new idea.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Insert Interval
leetcode.note: The closest public problem to Q9. Identical merge-on-insert logic. The difference is what is returned: 57 rebuilds and returns the list in O(n); Q9 must keep a **running covered total** so the query is O(1) and the insert stays O(log n). LeetCode 715 Range Module (Hard) is the version that keeps state across calls.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Edit Distance
leetcode.note: Q8 fixes the cost model to one substitution per step and asks for the shortest path, so it is BFS. 72 allows insert, delete and replace and asks for a distance, so it is DP. **Q8’s third follow-up - letters may be added or removed - is exactly the bridge**: adjacency becomes "edit distance 1", and the dictionary graph now links words of different lengths.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Minimum Window Substring
leetcode.note: Same two-pointer window as Q3, with a much harder validity predicate (a multiset of required characters rather than a count of zeros). If Q3 feels easy, this is the one that proves you understand *why* the left pointer never moves backwards. Reader-reported independently.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Merge Sorted Array
leetcode.note: The two-pointer merge, in its simplest form. Related to Q17 only in instinct - walk two inputs together rather than concatenating and re-sorting. Q17 merges by key, not by order.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Same Tree
leetcode.note: The lockstep two-tree recursion that Q17 is built on. Same Tree returns a bool at the point where Q17 returns a merged node, and it is worth writing once to see that the shape is identical.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Binary Tree Zigzag Level Order Traversal
leetcode.note: Level-by-level processing, measured from the **root**. Q10’s levels are measured from the **leaves**, which is why BFS does not work for it and a post-order pass does. Doing both back to back is the cleanest way to feel that difference.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Word Ladder
leetcode.note: The same problem as Q8. **One difference that will cost you marks if you miss it:** LeetCode 127 returns the number of *words* in the sequence; Q8 as stated returns the number of *transformations*. For hit → cog those are 5 and 4. Say which you are returning. Two independent reports in the existing research.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Max Points on a Line
leetcode.note: No relation to the 17. Included here because it is the most likely public equivalent of *Minimize Points Distance*, one of the interviewdb titles whose statement is still unknown - a hint to follow, not a claim.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Binary Tree Upside Down
leetcode.note: Tree re-pointing rather than tree reading. The same care Q17’s side-heavy follow-up needs: reassign links in an order where nothing you still need has been overwritten. Reader-reported, with a noted variant using a 0/1 right child.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Intersection of Two Linked Lists
leetcode.note: Two traversals that must meet. The classic solution equalises the lengths first - the same instinct as Q5’s follow-up, where you expand the smaller frontier because the cost of a round is the size of the side you expand.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Isomorphic Strings
leetcode.note: A stronger link than it looks. Q11’s keypad signature is a character → class mapping used to build a canonical key; isomorphism checks whether such a mapping exists. Both are the "reduce to a canonical form, then compare in O(1)" move.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Kth Largest Element in an Array
leetcode.note: Selection by rank. Q13 keeps the k highest-ranked items alive under a capacity, which is the streaming form of the same question: a bounded structure that always knows its weakest member.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
leetcode.note: A separately tagged LinkedIn classic, not one of the 17. The BST version is the one where the answer is a single descent with no recursion needed.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
leetcode.note: Also a separately tagged classic. Already worked in the existing coding page, including the k-node follow-up.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Shortest Word Distance
leetcode.note: The one-shot version. Only interesting as the setup for 244.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Shortest Word Distance II
leetcode.note: The design lesson behind Q11 and Q13: **preprocess once, answer many queries cheaply.** 244 indexes word → positions; Q11 indexes signature → words. Reader-reported independently.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Paint House
leetcode.note: A weak link, stated as such. Both walk a line under an adjacency constraint, but 256 is DP over costs and Q14 is a greedy count. Do not use 256 to prepare Q14.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Graph Valid Tree
leetcode.note: Cycle detection plus connectivity. Q2 needs the *undirected* walk over every component; Q15 needs the *directed* one, where a cycle means a back edge to a node still on the current path. 261 is the cleanest place to get the undirected version right.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Closest Binary Search Tree Value
leetcode.note: A separately tagged LinkedIn classic, not one of the 17.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Closest Binary Search Tree Value II
leetcode.note: Follow-up to 270: the k closest, which turns a descent into an in-order walk with a bounded deque or heap. A genuinely good LinkedIn question; just not one of the 17.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Integer to English Words
leetcode.note: A separately tagged classic. Pure case analysis; no relation to the 17. Worth one rep because it is almost entirely about decomposing the problem cleanly, which is what the Staff Coding module says it scores.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Find the Celebrity
leetcode.note: A separately tagged classic, already worked in the existing coding page. Reader-reported.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
leetcode.note: **Q17’s first follow-up, exactly.** 297 is the binary case with positional children; Q17 needs keyed children with unique sibling keys, which changes what has to be written: a key per child and a child count or terminator, rather than null markers.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Number of Connected Components in an Undirected Graph
leetcode.note: Q2 fails on hidden components if you only walk from one start node, which is the mistake 323 is designed to catch. Same outer loop over every unvisited vertex.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Reverse String
leetcode.note: A warm-up. Listed for completeness; no relation to the 17.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Top K Frequent Elements
leetcode.note: Map plus heap - the two structures Q13 combines. 347 counts then selects; Q13 must keep the selection correct while items arrive and leave.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Nested List Weight Sum II
leetcode.note: **The strongest non-obvious link in this table.** 364 weights each element by depth measured *from the bottom*, which is precisely what Q10’s peel round is. Both need one pass that computes height bottom-up rather than passing depth top-down. Reader-reported independently. (Supplied twice in the list.)
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
leetcode.note: The same structure as Q12: list plus index map, swap-with-last on delete. Q12 replaces GetRandom with **RemoveRandom**, which is the composition of the two and needs no new idea. LeetCode 381 is the duplicates-allowed version, which is Q12’s follow-up and is Hard. Reader-reported.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Shuffle an Array
leetcode.note: Fisher-Yates. Related to Q4 and Q12 through the same demand: every outcome equally likely, and a plausible-looking shortcut that is subtly biased. The classic wrong shuffle picks any index rather than one from the unshuffled tail.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: All O`one Data Structure
leetcode.note: The hardest of the "ordered structure in O(1)" family, and reader-reported. It is the right preparation for the Q13 follow-up where ranks stop being static: buckets of equal-count keys in a doubly-linked list, which is also how LFU is built.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: LFU Cache
leetcode.note: Same cache skeleton as Q1 and Q13; only the eviction key changes - frequency instead of recency, TTL or rank. Reported twice in the existing research, once with a **GetRank()** method and LRU as the tiebreaker, which sits almost exactly between Q1 and Q13.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: The Maze
leetcode.note: BFS where generating the neighbours is the work - the ball rolls until it hits a wall. Q8 has the same shape: the neighbour function (wildcard buckets) is where the thinking goes, not the search. Reader-reported and already worked in the coding page.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Random Pick with Weight
leetcode.note: The **mirror image of Q4**. 528 turns a uniform source into a biased one (prefix sums plus binary search); Q4 turns a biased source into a uniform one (debiasing plus rejection). Prepare them together - being able to go both ways is what the question is really testing.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Merge Two Binary Trees
leetcode.note: The binary case of Q17: overlap and the values are summed, otherwise the non-null node is used. Q17 generalises it in the direction that matters - children identified by **key** rather than by position, so child lookup becomes a dictionary probe and "absent branch" becomes a real case. Reader-reported, and the reader’s own note already describes the n-ary keyed variant.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Exclusive Time of Functions
leetcode.note: A stack over a log of start/end events. Shares Q6’s nesting discipline and Q7’s time-ordering, without the concurrency.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Max Area of Island
leetcode.note: **A name collision, not a match - check this before you revise it.** 695 is 2-D flood fill over a grid. Q3 "Artificial Island" is a 1-D sliding window with a conversion budget. They share only the word *island*. The real public equivalent of Q3 is **1004 Max Consecutive Ones III**, which is in the existing research as a reader-reported question.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Design HashMap
leetcode.note: Building the structure that Q11, Q12 and Q13 all use. Worth one rep so that "I would use a dictionary" is backed by knowing what the dictionary costs.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Building H2O
leetcode.note: Condition-variable signalling with nothing else in the way - the exact skill Q7 needs. In C# this is `SemaphoreSlim` or `Monitor.Wait`/`Pulse`; getting H2O right makes Q7’s wait loop obvious.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Design Bounded Blocking Queue
leetcode.note: The closest public problem to Q7 minus the delays. Same `lock` plus `Monitor.Wait`/`PulseAll` skeleton; Q7 adds a priority queue keyed on deadline and a **timed** wait, which is the part candidates get wrong.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Max Consecutive Ones III
leetcode.note: The actual public twin of Artificial Island: longest window with at most k zeros. Already in the existing research as reader-reported. **1004, not 695.**
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Possible Bipartition
leetcode.note: Literally Q2 with people instead of animals: a dislike list, split into two groups. The closest public statement there is.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Is Graph Bipartite?
leetcode.note: The same check given an adjacency list directly, so it skips the "build a symmetric graph from a one-way map" step that Q2 hides its difficulty in.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Find Leaves of Binary Tree
leetcode.note: Exactly Q10. Reader-reported and already worked in the coding page.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Can Place Flowers
leetcode.note: Exactly Q14, flowers instead of theatre seats, same greedy and the same boundary traps.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Second Minimum Node In a Binary Tree
leetcode.note: **Exactly Q16’s tree** - LeetCode defines it as root.val = min(children), which is a tournament tree. Marked Easy only because LeetCode accepts an O(n) scan of every node; Q16 wants the O(h) walk down the winner’s path, which is the whole point.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Range Module
leetcode.note: Q9 with removal as well, and the honest difficulty rating for maintaining merged intervals across calls. If Q9 goes well, this is the follow-up they reach for.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: LRU Cache
leetcode.note: The base Q1 extends. Reported in the existing research as an AI-round question, built with the assistant available.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
leetcode.note: Q12’s duplicates follow-up. Reader-reported and already worked in the coding page.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Implement Trie (Prefix Tree)
leetcode.note: The structure behind Q11’s prefix follow-up. Build it once by hand.
leetcode.label: lc

leetcode.title: Valid Parentheses
leetcode.note: Q6’s multi-bracket sibling. Tagged by LinkedIn in the six-month list; one 2025 report described a variant with integers and special characters, which is Q6.
leetcode.label: lc
